utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, to the interpreters. Good morning to the counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for Defence. Good morning, Witness DE. How do you feel today? Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you that you will continue to testify under an oath, and that you will continue answering questions that counsel for the Prosecution will be asking of you. Mr. McCloskey, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could show the witness the photo, Exhibit 807, which was what he was looking at before, followed up immediately by 178.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, this is the building that you looked at briefly yesterday and asked if you could get a wider-angle shot to help perhaps put it in perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so if we could now show the witness 178, and if we could put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, you may know, but this photo is shot roughly in the area in front of the school looking down towards the intersection, and the building in the previous exhibit should be in the middle of the screen. It's in a set of three buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be the building in question, the one that I spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And could you, could you take the pointer and point at the building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, for the record, it's the building in the centre of the photograph with the red roof, and we can see a white part of the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what building is that or was that in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was in the building while I was on leave, but I could tell you some history of that building. The command quarters, that is the MUP, wanted to have a facility in that area, and they used that building, that facility, only from time to time when they carried certain activities in the area; that is, when MUP carried such activities. So I don't know whether in that period of time the building was occupied or not. However, during the period of time when MUP engaged in certain activities, it was; however, when there were only checkpoints, I don't think that the building was occupied. And I don't know what happened after that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got back to Konjevic Polje after returning from Serbia, do you know what that building was used for when you got back? Because you said you spent a couple of days in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a couple of days in Konjevic Polje, and as to the purpose for which the building was used at the time, I didn't manage to learn, but in view of a longer period of time, I know that the building was used from time to time, occasionally; and the Banja Luka MUP had some training, some kind of training there, and they were placed in the school building that we had talked about yesterday, but that had happened some time ago. At any rate, some representatives of the MUP happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period before you left to Belgrade, what MUP organisation was using that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We referred to it as a MUP building, but its use was not very well defined. It all depended on the activities carried out in the area, and I don't know who decided as to who would be quartered there and when they would leave because that was the responsibility of the MUP. It probably depended on the most senior unit that was engaged in the area. That unit would probably be accommodated in that building. But mostly it was not occupied, so it was occupied only from time to time in peak periods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the most senior MUP organisation? Was it MUP Zvornik, MUP Bratunac, Special Army MUP, MUP from Janja? What was the actual MUP organisation that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the organisations that you have just numbered passed through Konjevic Polje during that period of time while I was there in one fashion or another. Even when the school was functioning, even when they were there, the minister of MUP came to visit it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it could have been any of those MUPs that I've mentioned that was using that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was quite possible. I personally don't know, because I wasn't there, so I don't know who used it. Any of the MUP organisations could use it. But there must have been a level at which a decision would be reached as to who would use the building, but I don't know about that, just as I told you yesterday when I said that I didn't know who would use the school building, but there must have been someone who decided as to who would use those facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring you back to the photograph, do you see your command and your communications building in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the two buildings in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed at the buildings on the far side of the photograph with the trees in front of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the building with the taller roof, which one is that again? Is that command or communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of an officer from the 65th Protection Regiment with the nickname of Cica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commanding officer for the 65th Protection Regiment was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the person, but I cannot remember his name. It's just not coming to my mind. I didn't have any special contact with him, but I know him from stories. I cannot remember his name, but I know the individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it Savic or Savcic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savcic, yes. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have a nickname of Cica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that nickname. I cannot answer your question. I never heard that the two names were linked, Cica and Savcic, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have a moustache?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savcic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he does. I say I don't think that he does because, you know, people sometimes wear a moustache, sometimes not. I knew Savcic, but not very well, and I don't remember seeing him with a moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the photograph, this photograph was taken, I believe, a few years after the events. Could you look down towards the intersection? And perhaps if we could move the photograph so we can see the left side. I believe this photograph shows what is now a petrol station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That photograph doesn't show a petrol station. I told you that I had repaired practically all facilities in Konjevic Polje. This is one of such facilities that I had intention to repair, but the level of destruction was rather high. The petrol station you're talking about is further down, and the facility in question is still as it is, as it is on the photograph. But you cannot see the petrol station because of this building, and the intersection is further down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there used to be a warehouse back in July of 1995 on the intersection where there is now a petrol station, right on the banks of the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There used to be a very old building, a very old facility there on that spot, but it didn't have any particular function; on the location where the petrol station is. It was an older building, but I don't think that it had any particular purpose or function. All I know is that the right to use the building belonged to the agricultural association, to the cooperative, from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same agricultural cooperation that owned the Kravica warehouse? The agricultural warehouse is in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never discussed it with anyone. I didn't even know who the head or the chief of the agricultural cooperation was, and I really don't know whether there's any link between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've told us that you were able to talk to people that were in this area at the period of time of July 13th. I want to -- and counsel asked you about Witness S. I want to tell you a brief story, and tell me if you have heard any parts of this particular story. It involves Muslim prisoners. Witness S, one particular Muslim prisoner, was taken prisoner in the morning of July 13th near the school that we've referred to earlier in Konjevic Polje, and he was taken to the little brick building that you've identified in front of the school as the reception building. He was placed in that building with other Muslim prisoners and was then taken to the front of your command and communication buildings near those apple trees, where he was interrogated by four men in army uniforms in the presence of police officers. And after his interrogation at your command building and your communications building, he was then taken over to the building you have described as the MUP building, and he was taken inside that building. And there were police officers in there, and one of the Muslims that was in that building with him was beaten by those police officers. Then he was taken with others down to this other building near the intersection that you've described as an old building belonging to the agricultural cooperative whereupon a bus came, and he was put on a bus with 15 other individuals, taken a short trip up the road to the Jadar River where he and others were taken out by soldiers with automatic weapons, taken down by the river, and executed. He was shot in the back and dropped into the river, and was able to be freed because the river took him away. Do you ever hear any stories resembling the story I just told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, I can give it some thought in the context of what I have already spoken about. I don't know who was in the school building. As regards the little building that I identified at the entrance, it was a small building that I had constructed where one of the units of the 65th Protected Regiment was located, but prior to the events that you have described. And that is where people would come, where families of the soldiers would come when they visited them. And I was involved in the construction of that reception. So I'm thinking as a military man. If the capture was carried out by a member of the police, and if the individual was brought to the school, that is, to the vicinity of this building, that means that it was done by the police, that he was in the custody of the police. And I think that in view of that period of time, Simanic was not there because he had gone away with the wounded towards the Vis feature. That happened on the 13th of July. So I don't think that any of the commanding officers were there from my unit. So it is possible that the man in question was sitting there or standing in this area. It was a small clearing where one could wait, and that is roughly all I can tell you about this story. I have never heard such a story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 13 July from Nova Kasaba to Konjevic Polje to Kravica, thousands of Muslim prisoners were taken by forces of the VRS. And you've never heard anything about that from your colleagues in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday what I heard, and I heard that in the area between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba there had been some fierce fighting with the view of intercepting the column, so that there must have been a smaller blockade because one part of the column was moving towards Cerska, and the other arm of the column went towards another location, so they were sort of surrounding Konjevic Polje. I told your colleague that I had learned about these events in Belgrade, and the first thing that I learned about was through a video clip which could be seen on one of the independent TVs in Belgrade, and it showed some captured people on a football pitch. It was a video footage that I saw in Belgrade in one of the independent TV stations. But as regards your specific question, I really don't know because I didn't see, and I didn't have an opportunity to discuss it. That the whole area was in a state of chaos, yes; everybody was describing that chaotic situation on the road. There were many people moving in columns, that the roads were full, and that took awhile. But as regards the 13th of July, I think that the fighting was still ongoing, and it is not possible that any transfer would have happened during that period of time because the fighting was really fierce at the time. I read the article of your expert, Butler, in a newspaper where a mention is made of three or four elite units of VRS that carried out the blockade and -- so, so it must be that the fighting was very fierce if somebody had to bring in elite units to intercept the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any fierce fighting on that video that showed the people on the football pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't say that it was on the football pitch. I'm talking about the area where the column was passing and about the attempts to deblock Konjevic Polje and to establish some kind of line towards the depth of the territory. It is perfectly normal and logical for such a formation to have -- to carry out a two-pronged attack. I didn't speak about the football pitch; I only told you that I had seen a video footage that was shown on TV, and where I saw some prisoners, and the cameraman identified that location as being a playground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In around the middle of August in 1995, did you receive additional support in the way of men from the Milici, Bratunac, and Zvornik brigades for construction and engineering projects?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. If you could be more specific and tell me which project you have in mind. I spoke about a number of projects. I don't know exactly which one you have in mind. But let me tell you another thing which is perhaps also -- can be also placed in that context, but I don't remember the exact time when it happened. My unit was substantially reinforced sometime during that period because a major construction work had started in the meantime on the waterworks in Han Pijesak. An infantry unit abandoned a theatre of operation in Krajina out of protest, and they reached Konjevic Polje together with some other units. And that unit was forcibly stopped, and they were handed over to me, and they were supposed to be used for some construction work because they were against war, or something like that. And I don't remember any other unit. And this whole company stayed in Han Pijesak all the time, and it was involved in the construction of the waterworks. I think that the strength of the unit was around 50 or 60 soldiers, maybe more. I don't remember the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they from the Zvornik, Milici, and Bratunac brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They may have passed through some kind of documents before they reached me. They were infantry men, according to their speciality, but I don't remember. And anyway, these were people from the Krajina who, together with the people who were withdrawing, were among the first to arrive, and they left the areas out of protest. They had had enough of war, and they reached this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now show the witness Exhibit 812.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is an exhibit that's an order from the Drina Corps, dated 17 August, signed by General Krstic, providing you with additional men from the Milici, Bratunac, and the Zvornik Brigades for various projects, including bricklayers, carpenters, machine operators, things like that. If you could just take a look at it. I don't -- we don't -- the subject matter is not necessarily important, but perhaps this will refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite possible. I can comment on it immediately, but let me look at the document first. Because I kept trying to get more people: builders, bricklayers, carpenters. That was our constant request. Now, whether we got them or not is another matter. This has refreshed my memory a little. There were several orders of this kind with respect to my Engineering Unit. I told you that the process of developing the battalion was hard and took some time, so that certain orders had to be executed, and it was difficult to say "I cannot carry it out" for this or that reason. But I do remember this order now. A small section of the Milici Brigade did reach me. From the Vlasenica Brigade, I don't think I got many; one or two bricklayers, one carpenter; and I got nothing from the Zvornik Brigade. I must underline that there were many orders of this kind. Every commander was trying to develop its own Engineers Unit, but without success. It says here "one construction technician, construction engineer, construction technician, plumber," and so on. Apart from my deputy, who was a construction engineer, and he was a reservist, we never had a technical person in the unit who could engage in these activities, so he never actually joined us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says you were supposed to get from Zvornik three construction machinery operators and two drivers; and from the Bratunac Brigade, four construction machinery operators, labourers, bricklayers, and other things. So did you ever get those machine operators or was this order not carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was partly carried out. I did receive something from the Milici Brigade. However, there were two operators among them, and I think one electrician, auto electrician - that is the first time I got one - and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went into Srebrenica after the -- shortly after the fall of the enclave. About what month was that that you went in to take care of a problem that was in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go immediately after the fall of the enclave, but upon my return from Belgrade, I told you, I arrived at Konjevic Polje. I stayed there for a day or two, the time it took to transfer what was available to Vis, because I said that was my major assignment. And then at Vis I received an order through the operations officer on duty from the Corps Commander to report in Srebrenica and to help the civilian authorities who were cleaning up the town regarding the problem of the river and all the facilities on it and the collector that I described yesterday. At the same time, there was an order to demine the zone of Srebrenica, primarily removing minefields in front of the former positions of the Skelani Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what month was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was around -- it was the month when these events occurred, so I think it was the 27th. That was the first time I went there. I think it could have been the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many mosques were there in Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I went to Srebrenica for the first time in my life then, though I'm born not far from there, but as a young man I went to military schools and I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who destroyed the mosques shortly after the fall of the enclave? Was it the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that the mosques from Srebrenica were destroyed after the fall of the enclave, though, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that. I did not give the matter much thought, nor was I in a position to do that. I carried out my orders. And believe me, I spent very little time in Srebrenica myself. I may have been there for a day or so, but we were addressing technical problems that we had to deal with. And then another day I spent in the area where we had to do the demining in front of the former positions of the Skelani Battalion, so that really I don't know. I simply don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, is there any mosque standing anywhere in the former Zvornik Brigade or Bratunac Brigade or Skelani Brigade or Milici Brigade areas of responsibility? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we show the witness Exhibit 646/A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, while they're getting that, did you learn of any murders of Muslim refugees coming out of Srebrenica or murders of Muslim prisoners taken from the column that left Srebrenica on July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard through the media. I told you that I saw that TV clip of some captured soldiers in a football pitch, and that was as much as I was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from any Drina Corps soldiers after you returned from Belgrade about the killings of Muslim prisoners from the column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are asking me about the Drina Corps. I have nothing to do with the command of the Drina Corps, nor any possibility to talk to them, because the focus of the activities of the Drina Corps at the time was the Zepa operation and the battles in that area. So I went towards Vis, which is in quite a different direction. So I had -- I was not in a position to have any kind of contact with people from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard from any VRS soldiers that Muslim people from Srebrenica were murdered by the VRS after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe Muslim soldiers were murdered by the VRS after the fall of Srebrenica as they came out and were captured and collected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was able to hear and read quite a bit about it from the media. And when I was invited by you for an interview, I read up a little more than usual, and those were the sources that I had access to that claimed that something had happened. I had no other specific information. However, the very fact, if it is true, for somebody who did not take part in it, simply avoided discussing it with anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe thousands of Muslim prisoners were slaughtered by the VRS after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that this question has been put to the witness already - it's still on the screen - and that the witness has answered the question. If they were killed, then they were probably slaughtered. I think it's just a question of the use of different words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe I -- the reason I asked that again is I don't believe he answered the first question about his beliefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask him whether he knows, not whether he believes. You can ask the witness whether he knows, whether he has any knowledge of it. A witness has come to tell us here what he knows, not what he believes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe, I believe he has told us that he learned about it from the media, so I think he's answered that question. So I can go on to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, go on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could put on this exhibit, 646A, if you could go to the second page on that, and if we could zero in a bit on that. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is a log from the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Unit that shows the digging of an ULT 220, and I just want to ask you a very, I hope, simply question. Could you look down in the bottom of the second page where it says "total used fuel," and it says --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- it says 13.5 times 20, and equals 270. Now, is the 13.5, is that the number of hours that the ULT was working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen from further up the table --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the 20 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where it says "completed." So that is the sum of what is stated up there, to get to the total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the 20 that is noted down at the bottom, is that -- does that refer to 20 litres of diesel fuel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, per hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit 709/A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we get to that next exhibit, Witness, what kind of big dump trucks did the VRS have access to in July of 1995? What were the basic sizes of the kind of a dump truck used for -- normally for carrying sand and gravel, things like that? What size in cubic metres was the usual dump truck that you were able to use or others were able to use for construction purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It varied from one unit to another. I spoke yesterday about the way in which the Engineers Unit of the Drina Corps was formed. The brigade Engineers Units were formed somewhat earlier, and they were supplied by work organisations in the area, war booty, and what other sources they had, so that this differed from one unit to another. In my particular case, I had two trucks with a carrying capacity of four cubic metres, counting the size of the sides. These are FAP 13 trucks, F-a-p, very old ones, and in the former JNA they were about to be discarded and put out of use; whereas the other trucks were mostly civilian ones that could be found in the area that the brigade units used. So there were small trucks like mine, the two that I had, and larger ones that could be found in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the largest capacity in cubic metres that a dump truck in the area would be able to carry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take into account that in the area there was a bauxite mine, which was a very large mine, which had very large trucks of large carrying capacity; then we had large civilian companies like Romanija Road, Zvornik Putovi; then there were construction companies in each of the towns in the region; and the way in which they were engaged within the brigade or outside the brigade through some sort of representative offices at the level of municipalities that decided how they could be used for the needs of the army, so that the capacity of the area was quite considerable in terms of the availability of such equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For one of those big trucks, what would be the capacity in cubic metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is rather vague. I mentioned four as a minimum, and you could go up to, shall we say, 20 cubic metres; or if one were to use the mining trucks, they even had a larger carrying capacity than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do we have Exhibit 709A?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a brief look at that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen or heard of this order before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This order mentions five tonnes of D-2 diesel fuel. Is that five metric tonnes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five tonnes. A tonne is a unit of weight. We know how much that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there 1.000 litres in a tonne?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic, do you have any additional questions, or Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad, no questions? Madam Judge Wald? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw the video of the prisoners on the football pitch in Nova Kasaba while you were in Belgrade. That was the period between the 9th and the 20th; is that right? Sometime in that period you saw it on Belgrade video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I think there was an error in the interpretation, Judge Wald. You said "between the 9th and 20th of July," and the witness heard "between the 9th and the 12th," so maybe that was why he said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, do you remember approximately when you saw it in Belgrade, when you saw the video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't be very definite, but I think it could have been about the 15th, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's good. That's fine. You mentioned at one point that during your absence, and when you found out what had happened when you came back, that there was one contingent or unit of soldiers - and I don't remember which one - that came in on the 13th and then left again on the 14th for Zepa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know or -- do you know from having your people report to you what that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I do apologise. I don't know whether it was properly translated. I'm talking about my contingent which returned from Vis. On the 13th, the deputy went to fetch them because he didn't have people to man the guard posts, and they were pulled out of what they were doing on the 13th. They arrived on the 14th, and they left on the 15th. That would be roughly the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You may have answered it, but let me ask it again. That particular unit that was there just for that day that was pulled out, and they were all put on guard post duty? I mean, that was what they did all that day? The day that they were there, the day that they were there, they arrived -- well --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that my defence was very important, and I had six guard posts, and that three were down to a minimum regarding manning. So that when units were absent, they couldn't be covered. There was only the rear platoon that covered those three posts. So I engaged the guards that I mentioned. They were not real soldiers. They came by bus and held guard duty during the night, so to provide the circular defence that I had organised in the area I was in. So if 15 soldiers returned, roughly -- I can't be absolutely specific. Someone may have been on sick leave or something. But if there was about 15, then there was a possibility to cover four guard posts with them. I still didn't have enough men to cover the whole circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is: If, as you say, you saw this video of the football pitch and the captured soldiers on it around July 15th, when you came back to your post you didn't ask anybody any follow-up questions about that, what happened or what they knew about what happened to those soldiers -- or to those captured Muslim people that you had seen on the video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss that with anyone. Simply upon arrival in Konjevic Polje, I made a survey of the situation and then went on to Vis. I simply had no occasion to talk with any responsible person about the subject. That the situation was chaotic, everyone told me that; that there were columns of buses, of vehicles passing by; that at the intersection it was absolutely chaotic. And the people who were there did tell me that, but nothing more specific regarding those soldiers on the football ground, and they couldn't have told me anything. So this general idea what the situation was like in the area was conveyed to me in the sense that it was chaotic, but I never discussed any particulars with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Witness D, I have a few questions -- DE, I'm sorry. You spoke to us about the handing over of duty, and you told us that troops needed to be lined up to say goodbye to them. And if I understood you correctly, you added "when that was possible." Did I get you correctly? Did I understand that correctly? Is that what you said, that the line-up was made when it was possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superior officer writes an order, and in the order he specifies how this takeover will take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you. I want to know whether I understood well this particular phrase. I remember very well everything that you told us. "To line up the troops to say goodbye, when that was possible." Is that what you said or did I make something up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to focus on this phrase "when that was possible." What did you mean when you said that? "Line up the troops to say goodbye when possible."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime conditions, there are situations when that cannot be known, when it's impossible. How can you call a person on guard duty to be lined up? You can't have some people who -- there are always people that you can't line up in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So all these requirements - lining up the troops, having all the documents, to inspect the facilities, to find the appropriate people - maybe, if somebody -- is justified if somebody is taking over who knows nothing about the unit; am I correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because this is a formal and legal procedure. It has a legal meaning. When I became head of the engineers - I showed you a document - the people have to know when I come on tour or on a visit who I am for me to be able to go to the command, the command of the Drina Corps, somebody has to introduce me to my colleagues. He must familiarise me with the relationships within the command. I may have known all that, but the Prosecutor asked me yesterday about a document that I signed with a person who took my place. That is why we personally keep those documents, because that man may say, "No, that's not right. I haven't taken over the duty. I haven't signed the document. Show it to me."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You said that this is the legal way to proceed, but when it is possible. Does that legal rule apply? Isn't there a situation when there's a force majeure due to which you cannot proceed normally? You said "when it is possible." What about when there is a contingency situation or an exceptional situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When something like that occurs -- and it is quite possible that the procedure may not be fully observed. But then the question is: Why? What are the conditions when such a situation may occur? For instance, a person can be replaced on the spot, but the question is: Why, and how? What are the circumstances? Even the person who is taking over duty, he may insist on the procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still talking within the frameworks of rules and procedures. But imagine a situation as follows: that someone who is in charge of a unit, and there's an urgent situation, a battle; there's a battle going on. In the meantime, this official in charge of the unit falls sick or is killed in the battlefield. Is his deputy in a position to replace him without having to go through this whole procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is called representation. There's a legal situation when you are representing somebody. You don't have all the rights and duties stemming from a formal appointment. Even my appointment was representation. I'll tell you why: Because neither by rank nor by speciality, I hadn't completed the General Staff school, so I was not familiar with the legal procedures and other knowledge to acquire that title. So if you will look at the document, it says he "represents." So I continued to receive all the benefits of a battalion commander. You could see that from the record that I signed with the person who took over from me, my successor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but imagine your situation. You were responsible for a unit. You were responsible for the unit. You had a deputy who would normally replace you in your absence. You fall sick, and it is absolutely impossible for you to continue to head the unit. And this is a final impossibility, that's what I'm talking about. This deputy, your deputy, can he immediately assume command of the unit without having to wait this 15-day or 20-day period for the takeover? Just imagine that there's no person to carry that out, anyway. So your deputy, since you are absolutely incapacitated to continue in your position, can he immediately assume command, and then possibly wait for the formalities to take place subsequently? How do things happen in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that was the case with myself, due to the fact that I left the unit on the 9th and went to Belgrade. My deputy remained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry to interrupt you. I am not talking about the possibility of going to Belgrade and leaving the area. My hypothesis is of another nature, and I'm sorry to have to speak in hypothetical terms. Let's say that you were killed in battle and you -- it is physically impossible for you to come back. I'm sorry to interrupt you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a possibility of being automatically replaced. The commander of the 1st Platoon automatically replaces the commander of the company. The deputy of the battalion commander automatically replaces the battalion commander. But even if he should get killed, there must have been some kind of procedure for that person to assume the command from then on. There is a rule within a platoon, for example. When the platoon commander is killed, he is then replaced by the commander of the 1st Platoon, and then the new structure is immediately in place, and they're all familiar with that. So that exceptional situation must be legally resolved sooner or later. There would be a legal procedure later on. Even if the individual in question gets killed, a commission would be established later on to take care of the procedure, but he would be working all the time. However, the procedure formally speaking must be legally completed. There must be a beginning of the procedure, it is usually an order, and there has to be a record of the handover of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. When you spoke about the handover of duty you mentioned duties of the commander who is leaving, that is, the outgoing commander, who has the duty to transmit everything to the in-coming commander. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So does he also have to transmit secrets and any other type of confidential information to the in-coming official?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are certain things that even the commander is not aware of, talking about secrets. For example, on several occasions I was in a similar position. There is a service whose duty is to protect the military structure as a whole. And when I left Pale there was a commission that was established for that purpose because the commander thought, his assessment was, that I am not the kind of official who could leave without a commission having to review that procedure. And that was part of the Security Service. (redacted) is leaving, one has to see whether he has taken some documents with him as he left, whether there has been any abuse of office and similar things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will take care of that. You may continue, Witness DE.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether certain things could have been mishandled, whether it was possible for an abuse to have occurred, and that can also involve the commander. The commander can also erroneously carry out his assignments. You have probably read a lot about espionage during the Second World War. There are commanders who engage in activities which are prohibited to him and which can be lethal for the organisation, so there must be someone who will decide on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if the commander has the duty to transmit everything to the in-coming commander, it means that he has to transmit to him everything that is likely to be important for that person so as to maintain the level of organisation and command and control of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DE, let me go back to something that you have perhaps already answered in response to a question to Judge Wald, but let me try to clarify something. Do you know if that video clip that you saw in Belgrade around the 15th of July involving captured soldiers on a football pitch, do you know if it was possible to see that programme in the eastern part of Bosnia, in the area of Bratunac, Zvornik, Konjevic Polje, and so on? Was it possible for them to see that programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been very difficult. The programme belonged to one of the independent TV stations, and the official TV station wouldn't show that programme. And those independent TV stations were covering the area of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question involving your travel to Srebrenica. Did you actually enter the centre of the town, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the town of Srebrenica. It would be very difficult for me to locate the centre of the town because I really don't know much about it. That was the first time that I entered the town, and I may have gone back on one other occasion, but that's it. My area of activities was towards the border, and I focussed in the area towards Tuzla and Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I should like to know whether you actually entered the town of Srebrenica. Let us leave the word "centre" out of the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was in town, in the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see any mosques?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understood, you went there on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts. Most probably on the 27th, but it's very difficult for me to be specific. It's been a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fall of Srebrenica, was it considered as a victory? Was it perceived as a victory by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, any facility that is taken possession of is considered as a victory, let alone the town of Srebrenica. But if you're talking about the tragedy that occurred, I must say that it was a very unfortunate event how things turned out, and I am also referring to the International Community as well, because the area was only formally protected, but it actually constituted a military facility because of the problems that we had in the area. I myself, I am from the area of Milici, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you know what were the consequences of the fall of Srebrenica within the VRS, and what impact did it have on its soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very simple question, Witness. What was the effect on the soldiers of the VRS that the fall of Srebrenica provoked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean morally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exactly what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and answer your question. As far as I understood things as one of the commanders, I think that the very capture of Srebrenica, if we put aside the fact that it was a protected area, if it had been really a protected area, if it had not constituted, militarily speaking, a problem for us, it wouldn't have been any burden for us. However, we were holding our positions around the area all the time. It was very tiring, and people were very nervous, and every single rotation of the military brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sorry to interrupt you once again, but let us streamline the question. Did soldiers talk amongst themselves about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you about my soldiers and who participated in what. I practically didn't see them, so I do not have any particular insight in the fall of Srebrenica and the time that followed. But I know that Srebrenica had been a very problematic issue for us. It was a heavy burden for the corps, and we had sustained a number of losses before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it would have been normal for soldiers to talk about a victory amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must have been such talks, of course. I am sure about that. Yes, soldiers talked about a victory, and the feeling, the atmosphere was a victorious one. So militarily speaking the fall of Srebrenica was a victorious one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move to another area. We have spoken about the VRS soldiers, but I would like to know in follow-up to your question, what was the consequence of the fall of Srebrenica for the population that live in the surrounding area of Srebrenica? What were the consequences of that fall? So now I want you to talk about the population. What I asked you about soldiers I should like to know about the population that lived Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. around the area of the protected zone. What was the effect of what happened on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the Serbian population that lived outside the protected area or the Muslim population that lived within the area? Who do you have in mind: the Serb population living around the enclave or the Muslim population living inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the Serb population, the population of the Republika Srpska, who lived in the vicinity of Srebrenica, around the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they perceived the fall of Srebrenica as a great victory and final relief of a very heavy burden for them, because there had been a lot of tension on both sides of the line. The population was terrified; both communities were terrified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us try and simplify things. The people, the residents of the area, talked about the fall of Srebrenica amongst themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So was there a follow-up of the fall of Srebrenica, an interest in the follow-up of that fall? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but again I don't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to clarify my question. You told us that the residents of the area perceived the event as a victory and that that had been an objective of some kind. Now, I would like to know what happened with the population after those events. Were residents interested to know what would happen afterwards? Were they following the events that took place after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that there must have been individuals who were interested in that and those who were not. Not many things could be said publicly, in the open. What happened was really ugly, and I don't think that any normal person would take interest in them. I mean, we are all human. I don't think that they would have accepted it. So I don't think that it was really publicly discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go -- try and go back to my question. Before the fall of Srebrenica and after the fall of Srebrenica, certain events took place. Do you think that those events, those that had taken place before the fall and those that took place after the fall, were they important for that population, for that community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am somewhat confused as to the specificity of your question. I cannot be more specific than I am, or maybe I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe you think that I have actually another question in mind, but no. I just want to know whether the events that had taken place before the fall of Srebrenica and the events that took place after the fall of Srebrenica, do you think that those events were interesting for the population that lived around the area? Do you know -- do you think that they wanted to know whether they had any interest in those events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean whether those events were linked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I'm referring to the interest of the population in those events.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I understand your question now. The misfortune of Srebrenica is a misfortune that befell both the Serbian and the Muslim population, and any war as such is a great tragedy. The people who lived there, the people who were divided because of that zone, were under a very heavy burden and fear of the conflict and of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know about that. Let me ask you a specific question: What was the type of relationship between the soldiers and the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That relationship was excellent. The residents of the area were actually soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that at one point you mentioned something about the cooks in your unit, and you said that they were female.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they soldiers? Were they professional soldiers, members of the army, or civilians who were preparing food for the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were civilians. They came by bus from Milici and they returned home every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You told us that the relationship between the soldiers and the population was excellent. Now I would like to know if it was possible for the population to know what was happening, what kind of manoeuvres were being carried out and what kind of objective the army had in mind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume if somebody wanted to find out, they would probably know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not talking about military secrets, of course, but what could be seen publicly. So there was a good relationship. You said it was an excellent relationship between the army and the population, which means that the population could see and know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it possible for the population to ask the soldiers, for instance, what happened somewhere in a particular place? Was it possible that the population could ask a soldier a question of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was possible. I have no further questions, Witness DE. Thank you very much for coming here, for coming to testify, and we wish you a safe journey home, and have a good day. The usher is going to pull down the blinds. Please don't move, so that you may leave safely. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask when I mentioned my name that it be somehow redacted, when I mentioned my name inadvertently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's already been regulated. Don't worry. Fine. It's all right. There won't be any problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Your Honours, and I wish you success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know whether we should take advantage of the presence of the witness in order to tender some documents, or can we do that afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the presence of the witness is not necessary. My idea was to have a break now and then come back, as we have many things to deal with. But Mr. McCloskey, what do you think? Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is one issue, Your Honours, that relates to a specific exhibit that was tendered by -- or presented by this witness, and if I can find the exhibit itself. I believe it's 142, which is an exhibit that appears to have missing from the top part of the exhibit the normal features that we have seen on every other order that has been issued by representative units of the VRS. In respect of this particular exhibit, we would request that the Trial Chamber make an order that the complete document be produced. Since this witness is here and since this witness had access to it, we would ask the Court to direct the Court Order to this witness, as well as to the Defence, that the complete document be submitted to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecutor before the conclusion of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we haven't finished after all, Witness DE. We have a minor problem to deal with. Do you have the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. If I may explain very briefly. The document pursuant to which this document was issued, the document of the Superior Command, was submitted to you, and I think you have admitted it, and that is the document on which this document is based. And in the left-hand upper corner there is no information about registration. Those would be the information that my unit would have to put down, that is, where the document was registered. So I must repeat that this document may have not been registered, because these are personal copies. But I can provide an original -- the original document. So in the preamble it says that it is pursuant to another document which is much more important, the document ordering me to go to the place of representation. So this is a document that I need to have should my successor say that something is not in order, or vice versa. But there's no problem. I can provide the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, it is possible to get the document of which this is a copy, and you promise to provide this document to us. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel, have you any remarks to make regarding this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Let us just take upon ourselves the obligation that if the witness provides us the original, we will hand it in to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that all right, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness DE, finally, you may leave now and you may go back home, and I think things will work out well for you too. So we're now going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we now have to address the question of admission into evidence of a series of exhibits. There are the exhibits from the testimony of General Krstic -- I don't know whether I'm wrong -- so from the Defence, as we are talking about the Defence case now, so let us hear the Defence first. Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution. During the examination of General Krstic, the Defence used a whole series of documents, and over the past few days, together with the Prosecution, we have come to an agreement which, in brief, is the following. The documents from D25 -- no, I'm sorry, from D27 up to D73 and pursuant to the list marked D135, which has been provided to the Registry, the Defence and the Prosecution have come to an agreement and that is that because of the need to check the authenticity of these documents, which will be done during the continuation of the Defence case, as these are mostly exhibits which are exhibits coming from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, orders of the 2nd Corps and the 28th Division of the BiH army, and we have explained how we have come into the possession of those documents. And in order to remove any ambiguity, we need a little more time to provide evidence of the authenticity of these exhibits, that is, from D27 to D73. I'm sorry, I'm wrong, up to D71. So D27 to D71. Also, through contacts with Mr. Harmon, reservation has been expressed regarding document D74, D74. But it is a document which General Krstic identified as his own document, a document which he dictated the contents of; but it is a fact that the second page of that document is missing, which bears his name and surname, which probably, due to technical reasons, was not photocopied. But the Defence has in its possession the original version of that document so that in the further course of the proceedings, during the next sitting, it will provide the complete document. Between the parties, that is the Defence and the Prosecution, there was no dispute over documents starting from 76 -- 74 through to and including 134, bearing in mind the fact that this is a list marked for identification as D135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Petrusic. This set of documents over which there is no dispute, the translation I received, that it concerns document D74 to 134, but we know that document -- Defence document 74 was one that the Prosecution expressed reservation over because the second page is missing with his signature, et cetera, so you're going to address that separately. So it would be logical that this set of documents over which there is no dispute should begin with the number 75. That's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From 76, you're quite right, Mr. President. The documents from 76 through to 134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have one additional observation to make, Mr. President. With regard to documents from the list D135 that bear the numbers 79, 81, and 109, the Defence would like to note that those documents do not have a revised version of the English translation attached. So those would be the exhibits that the Defence has used during the testimony of General Krstic and the documents on which the parties have agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Petrusic, with regard to document 79, 81, and 109, I see on the list document 135. If you look at 79, we have 79A, English translation of D -- 79B. The same applies to document 81A, which is the English translation, and the same to document 109. We have an English translation. So we have the English translations mentioned, and you are telling us that we don't have an English version of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the first English version, which did not need revisions at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see. I understand. Is that all, Mr. Petrusic? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The documents that my colleague has referred to that has a part of the document that has been cut off, and the document to which we objected in our discussions, is not document 74 but Prosecutor's -- Defence Exhibit 97. And if my colleagues refer to Defence Exhibit 97, I'm sure they will see that 97 was the subject of our discussion and our agreement. So when my colleague said that we had an objection to 74, we do not have an objection to 74. It is instead to document 97, which was the document that we had agreed would be not tendered at this point in time, subject to additional clarification on that document. In respect of the other documents my colleague mentioned, that there are English translations attached to all of these documents, those, as Your Honours will recall, were the English translations, unofficial English translations that were submitted by my colleagues. All of those documents have been subsequently submitted to the Language Service Section for official translations, because we all agree that the matter of translation, and accurate translation, is fundamental to assessing the evidence. And we have submitted to the Language Service Section all of the documents that have been submitted by the Defence from Defence Exhibit 76 on, and it is my understanding that the revisions, with very few exceptions, have been completed and have been submitted to the Registrar at this point. However, to make it perfectly clear, I have a set of those revisions, as do my colleagues, and those have been renumbered by us and provided to my colleagues as, for example, D76, the revised translation would be D76A bis. But I have a set of these revisions for the Defence exhibits, and I'd be prepared at this point in time to submit these to the Registrar so the record is perfectly clear that they have received revisions as to all of the exhibits, with the exceptions of the ones that my colleague has identified. So I have these here, and if I could make the submission to the Registrar, the record will be perfectly clear on that point. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I think that the only point we need to clarify is the Defence document 96 [as interpreted] which is objected to, and not D74.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I should like to first of all thank Mr. Harmon. It is indeed document 97, for which we will provide further evidence of authenticity, and not Exhibit 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is the original version that you will produce at a future hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Photocopies, a photocopy of that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Registrar, on the part of the Registry, are there any difficulties or are things clear?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The things are clear, as far as the Registry is concerned, but I would like to know whether the revised translations have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They certainly have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the only clarification that was necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I should touch upon the issue now, because we are talking about evidence for General Krstic, but I would like to know whether the exhibits that were produced during this week have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will deal with them now, I think. So Mr. Petrusic, or Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there were some Prosecution exhibits related to General Krstic which, since we're on the subject of General Krstic, we might want to deal with those also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're right, Mr. McCloskey. I also mentioned it. You are very efficient, obviously, Mr. McCloskey. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have identified those Prosecution exhibits in a three-page document which has been marked as Exhibit 837, which both the Defence and the Registry have. And just to -- so I won't go through all the exhibits, but to clarify one or two points: Apparently I mentioned Exhibit 367, which was a revised or extended version of a video, and I'm told that that was actually -- should have been 367 bis, to clarify the record. And also, we have put in a revised version of the video of General Mladic and others coming through Srebrenica. This is Exhibit 145/1. This is revised to include the various segments in our possession to try to make it as complete as possible. And on the second page of Exhibit 837 we have Exhibit 792A and B. That's the Bratunac Brigade daily combat report dated August 4th that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deals with the subject of General Krstic and President Karadzic being in Srebrenica. There has been some discussion over the appropriate translation of that, and Defence counsel and the Prosecution have been in discussions with the Language Services Unit and have been told that they are going to provide a brief memo on that topic to try and clarify the translation of that particular document. So I would offer that material into evidence. I don't believe there's any objections on that particular set of documents. In addition, we are offering the exhibits that were mentioned near the end of the last time we saw General Krstic on the witness stand, and that regarding the statements about the phone book and the mother's death certificate. And the first exhibit in that group is Exhibit 836/1, the memo of Dean Manning regarding the personal property and other property. Then 836/2, the receipt Mr. Manning provided to Christian Rohde regarding that property. Then 836/7, Christian Rohde saying he provided that material to General Krstic. Then 836/6, the complete listing of material obtained from General Krstic at his arrest. Then 836/5 is the group of personal medical documents that were provided to General Krstic shortly after his arrest. Then 836/4, a document in B/C/S regarding a medical instruction. And then 836/3, a copy of more personal medical information. And it is my understanding that the Defence does want to discuss those materials, and Mr. Harmon is prepared to enter in that discussion, and I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you very much. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, from the list 837 which contains the documents that my learned friend has referred to ending with document 803A and B, the Defence has no objection regarding those documents. However, when it comes to the whole document 836, which is not on this list and which my learned friend has referred to, the Defence would like to object to this document on the following grounds. When this document was submitted, 836/1, the Defence pointed out that these were personal effects; therefore, things that can have nothing to do with the criminal charges, nor can they have any connection, nor can any criminal or legal conclusions be made regarding participation, aider or abettor, or any other role that may be attributed to General Krstic. If the purpose of this document -- Mr. President, I do apologise for perhaps very briefly entering into an analysis of this. This is certainly something that should be addressed in the closing argument, but allow me to say a couple of sentences about it. If the purpose of tendering document 836/1, that is, the telephone notebook, was to check the credibility of some witnesses whether certain numbers were in the phone book or not, then that aim has been fulfilled because I think there was no dispute regarding those numbers. However, it is my submission that such a document, a personal document, cannot be used for the purpose of verifying the credibility of a witness. Whether it was written in 1991 or maybe dates back to the 1980s, who knows? This is something that was confiscated in 1998. So this is a document that is constantly changed; one adds new numbers and so on. So I would like to retain my position and my objection to this document. Also, when we're talking about 836/2 through to 7, the position of the Defence is that those documents also can only in no way be used as evidence in this case. We had a great deal of discussion over certain things in that connection which really should be a question to be discussed between the Registry, the Prosecution, and Defence counsel, rather than for the trial record. And I'm referring to this particular exhibit. If we are now discussing these things, and mention has been made many times of this unfortunate death certificate, I will continue to uphold the position that that is something that needs to be resolved by the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Registry amongst themselves. But I would like to underline that as far as I know, that death certificate is not original -- or rather, the original document has not been restored to the owner, but let us leave that aside. The Defence also upholds objection with regard to these documents marked under 836/1 through 7, and that is the only objection that the Defence has regarding this list carrying the number 837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could first comment on the subject of the personal phone book that counsel mentioned. That personal phone book was not amongst the exhibits that I mentioned. It's my understanding and memory that the material from that phone book came in, as we had agreed and -- or as the Court had ordered, if I remember correctly, and that's all we intend to do in that matter based on our previous -- the previous ruling. And of course both sides will be free to argue, so I won't get into the argument here. And on the other material and the death certificate, Mr. Harmon will address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to clarify: Who has the notebook now? The Registry, or who?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We gave a copy of the notebook shortly after that to the Defence, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Who has the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe the Evidence Unit actually has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Of the -- of yours, of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of our Evidence Unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you have a problem with giving it back? I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The actual physical notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As an exhibit with people's names in it who may be involved in future cases, it's the kind of thing that the Prosecution would like to keep. However, there's never been any problem with the Defence examining all of these items, as is normal, and getting any kind of copy that they may need in certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But I gather, or at least I understand that it's a matter that the General wants his notebook back, I think, or -- so I guess that's a question of whether or not your physical custody of it is what's at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see Mr. Harmon moving around next to me, so I think I'll let him address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Wald, I can address your concern. Some of the items that were seized from General Krstic have evidential value, and it's our -- and we expect to continue to possess the originals.
