Most of the items that were seized from General Krstic have no evidential value, and we're prepared to give back the originals of those. But a decision as to what has evidential value will have to be made by the Office of the Prosecutor. There are some items I will not describe on the record, but we intend to keep the originals of those items. In respect of the other issues that were raised by my colleague, specifically, 836/2 through 836/7, I certainly agree with Mr. Petrusic. These are matters that should have been discussed between the Registry, between the Prosecutor's office, and between the Defence, rather than being made part of the trial record. The Prosecutor's office did not make the medical certificate -- or the death certificate part of the trial record. We did not make the medical records of General Krstic part of the trial record. Indeed, that issue was raised by General Krstic himself. And I can refer Your Honours to the transcript of these proceedings, page 6863, lines 20 through 24, in addition to which my colleague Mr. Petrusic raised the issue, prior to General Krstic raising the issue, at page 6856, lines 16 through 25. Both of those transcript cites are the English version of the transcript. So I fully agree with my colleague, Mr. Petrusic, that those should have been matters that were private and could have been regulated, but they weren't. And indeed, the impression that was left on the public who watched these proceedings and on the Office of the Prosecutor was that the Prosecutor's office was intentionally withholding matters from General Krstic despite his request. The record that we have submitted to Your Honours is to clarify that record. It is clear from the information that is contained in Prosecutor's Exhibit 836/2 through 836/7 that within days of the arrest of General Krstic, he had asked for certain items, copies of certain items were provided to him, a complete list of those items was provided to the Registrar. And I will say, I've been on this case for a considerable period of time, and not a single request has been directed to me for the return of any of those items. In fact, I am prepared, having confronted this issue for the first time publicly, and I have told my colleagues very clearly, that if they take the list that was the inventory of items and they highlight that list, we will -- and give that to me as to which items are requested by General Krstic, we will review that list, make a determination as to what of the items have evidential value and which do not, and we will return the original items to General Krstic. I will say now that it's our view that the medical records do not contain evidential value. We will return the originals of that. His mother's death certificate is not of evidential value to us. We are prepared to return that to General Krstic. But he has to tell us which of the originals he wants, and we will act accordingly. It's our position, therefore, that items 836/2 and 836/7 should be admitted into evidence. They are admitted -- and they should be admitted for purposes of clarifying the record that was raised initially by General Krstic and raised initially by his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm having problems. If they're admitted into evidence for -- even for the limited purpose you're talking about, then that means he can't get them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These are copies, Judge Wald. What is in the record are, first of all, copies. The originals he can get back. They have been retained by the Evidence Unit of the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you've made your statement, I think, very articulately, as to why he didn't get them back earlier, et cetera, so basically, why do we need them in the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, there is one issue that -- the Court can consider this issue, the issue of credibility of General Krstic. General Krstic said that he would like to have returned to him his telephone book, his medical records, including the death certificate of his mother. The inference from that statement is that he didn't get back the medical records or the death certificate of his mother. He did get a copy of them back. Had General Krstic said, "I'd like the original back," had he raised that issue, that would have been one matter. He didn't say that. And we believe that the documents that we have presented are relevant for - and the Court can give them whatever weight it deems appropriate, relevant to the issue of the credibility of General Krstic. Now, the Court -- if the Court does not deem them to have much weight, that's obviously a function the Trial Chamber must apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That takes away his right to privacy once they're in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to these documents being admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, with regard to the notebook, the telephone book you mentioned, if I understood rightly, that it has an evidentiary value for you, not only in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you'd like to keep it, even if he asks for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would like to keep the original of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And he can have the copy for his personal use?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's your stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we can all agree that the issue cannot be decided by the Chamber. It's an issue that has to be solved between the Prosecution and the Defence, and of course the Registry as well. Before we finish, I think that we need to address certain new elements that have arisen in the meantime, but I don't know whether Mr. Petrusic wanted to add anything to this discussion. The issue of personal effects must be resolved between the Registry, the Defence, and the Prosecution. But aside from that, is there anything that you would like to add, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nothing in particular, Mr. President, but let me just say that the parties here have difficulties in agreeing. The Prosecutor is saying, "Why not requesting those documents?" and we are saying, "Well, why aren't you giving us that which is considered as personal effects?" The photocopies have been the subject of evidence here, under seal, and they're probably going to be kept as such. However, the original documents, and this is what we're talking about, is something that we believe should be restored, regardless of a possible probative value for this case or for some other case. So obviously we have opposing views in this matter. We are requesting all documents -- we want all the documents to be restored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but once again, I'm must stress that the issue must be resolved by the Registry, and I hope that the Registrar will take note of our discussion today. Let us go back to the documents. Madam Registrar, is there any problem here for you as regards numbers or similar things?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, we don't have any problems with numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we will need to have a very urgent meeting regarding the issue that has just popped up involving personal effects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you will take care of that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Maybe the Registry and you will have to talk back and forth about the original, but we still have a legal question as to whether we admit, I mean, as to whether certain of these documents are admitted, as I understand it, and the Registry can't solve that for us. So that there seems to be, I think, two debates. One, can they get back certain of the original, physical, tangible objects. That's, I understand your position, not if they're of evidentiary value, but some you don't mind if they're not of evidentiary value. Okay, that can be settled between them. But your position is you want, in order for your argument on credibility, you want certain of the documents to be admitted, and do you oppose their admission? I just want to get that clarified. Leaving aside whether you get them physically back, do you oppose their admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards document 836/1 to 7, the Defence objects to the admission of that document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald, for clarifying the issue. I was about to consult with you on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having heard the arguments, and having considered all of the documents that have been mentioned, the Chamber shall order admission into evidence of several - and I hope things will be clear for the Registrar - documents, that is to say, all of the documents except for document number 97 which will be authenticated through a photocopy of the original document, and Prosecution documents 836/1 to 7 which will be subject of a separate ruling. The Chamber will therefore make a decision on this exhibit once it has analysed the whole situation. I hope things are clear for the parties. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, when you say you are admitting all of the documents except 97, does that mean that you are admitting all documents between Defence Exhibits 76B through the end of the list, because I don't believe the Defence has tendered Defence Exhibit D27 through Defence exhibit D74. Those were going to be the subject of an additional discussion. I just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think it will be more clear if we leave the decision for all of the documents because I think that there is a need to have another look at the documents. You are quite right, Mr. Harmon, I did not consider that set of documents which remains to be authenticated, I think. So it will be better to leave the decision for next week, including -- because in the meantime, the document 77 will be authenticated, and we hope that the photocopy of the original version will be presented to the Prosecution. So the document will be authenticated and the Chamber will have then an opportunity to reach a decision concerning all of the documents; otherwise, I think we risk leaving aside certain documents. Do you agree with this suggestion, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So having heard the remark of Mr. Harmon, I think we are all aware of the fact that it is necessary to have a careful look at the documents once again, and the Chamber will make its ruling during the week of the 4th of December. I don't know if there's anything else that you want to be considered at this point. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I have three exhibits to regulate. One is Prosecutor's Exhibit 765. Prosecutor's Exhibit 765 was a videotape of a negotiation in Zepa that was occurring with General Mladic, Muslim representatives, certain members of the Main Staff, and Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric. The Defence had entered an objection to it, the objection being they didn't know the source of the document, the date of the document, and when we received it. Well, I have subsequently gone back and I've ascertained that information. I've conveyed that information to my colleagues. The film was made by Republika Srpska Television in Pale. The film was provided to us by the Republika Srpska liaison officer on the 25th of February, 1998, and it depicts events that occurred in Zepa on the 19th of July, 1995. I have informed my -- I have informed my colleagues of this, and I have been informed that they have no objection. We would therefore seek admission of the film itself which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 765, and 765A and B which are the transcripts from that film. I have two additional exhibits which I'd like to regulate, but perhaps my colleagues should be heard on the issue of the admission of 765 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. first, and then I can turn to the next two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, did you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have two additional exhibits, Mr. President and Your Honours. One is Prosecutor's Exhibit 823, and that is an order of the Drina Corps command that is dated the 12th of May, 1995. And in the course of the examination of Witness DB on the 7th of November, he said that the paragraph 3 had been translated incorrectly, and I said to the Chamber that we would submit that to -- for a revision. That has been submitted for revision, and I would like to tender now Prosecutor's Exhibit 823A bis, which is the revised translation. Similarly, Mr. President and Your Honours, Prosecutor's Exhibit 830 is a -- was a document dated the 11th of July, 1995, and I had noted in the course of the examination that there was a problem in the signature block, and again I indicated that that would be revised. So that has been revised, and I'm not submitting to Your Honours and to my colleagues Prosecutor's Exhibit 838 bis, the revised translation, and I would now tender to the Court the revisions that I have just described. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, Exhibits 823A bis and 830, the last exhibits that the Prosecutor has just mentioned, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we can just have a quick look at the exhibit, that is exhibit number 830.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're not familiar with the exhibits yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we perhaps leave the issue of admission of these two exhibits for our next session? We would really like to have a closer look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was just about to suggest the same thing. Because we have postponed our decision, so you can tell us your position later on. Mr. Harmon, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I see Mr. McCloskey has something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a couple of Prosecution exhibits for the last witness. I think that the Defence has some exhibits for the last witness also. The Prosecution exhibits are Exhibit 807, which was the photo of the MUP building that was identified by the witness; and then Prosecution 812, which was the August order for more men and materials for the 5th Engineering Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, it's my mistake; I should have known that. But did you say 807A and -- 807 to 812, or only the two of them, 807 and 812, or the documents in between as well? No, I think that there is a problem with interpretation. Okay, it's been corrected. So are you tendering Exhibits 807 and 812, or [English] between 807 till 812? I think that -- [Interpretation] I think you wish to tender only two exhibits, but I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Correct, only two exhibits, 807 and 812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not object to these two exhibits that have been tendered by the Prosecution. However, I should like to take this opportunity and tender some of our exhibits: D137A and B, D138B, 139A and B, D140A and B, 141A and B, 143B, D144, D145, and D146. As regards Exhibit number D142A and B, it is a document for which the Prosecution has requested the original to be provided by the witness, and we will tender this particular exhibit together with the original. At the same time, the translations of documents that have already been tendered, 138 and 143, which have been tendered in their B version, that is, the original version, will be submitted later on, as soon as they are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, as regards the exhibits that have just been tendered by Mr. Visnjic, 137 to 146, I think -- 148 is also included, but without translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Mr. McCloskey? Also as regards the late submission of the translation? And you don't have any problem with the original version of the document 142 being tendered later on, once we get the original documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will consider all of these documents together. We're not going to make separate rulings. I think it is perfectly possible to admit documents 807 and 812 into evidence. But there are other things as well, so we will keep all of these documents together and they will be the subject of one decision of the Chamber. From the Defence, is there anything else that you would like to bring up?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All I can do at this point is to wish you a good weekend and a lot of success in your work, for those who intend to work during the weekend. And we will reconvene on the 4th of December, at the usual hour, that is, 20 minutes past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
